item.title: Extracting Fixed View Definitions From The Oracle Binary
item.description:
If you’ve ever needed to look up the definition of a dynamic performance view in Oracle, also referred to as a fixed view, or simply a V$ view, chances are that you’ve come across V$FIXED_VIEW_DEFINITION.

It is a special dynamic performance view that exposes the SQL definitions of Oracle’s V$ views in its VIEW_DEFINITION column, which is defined as VARCHAR2(4000), as shown by the output of describe (from version 23.26.0.0):

item.title: Bypassing oradebug Restrictions
item.description:
In Oracle 26ai, the execution of certain oradebug commands and actions is no longer possible, as Oracle has changed the default value of the undocumented parameter _disable_oradebug_commands from none to restricted.

This change causes some oradebug functionality to stop working, as previously discussed by Jonathan Lewis in this blog post. Moreover, Mikhail Velikikh noted in a comment on the blog post that the parameter change from none to restricted was already introduced in RU 19.24.

item.title: Printing Non-Null-Terminated Strings With GDB
item.description:
In C, a string is an array of characters terminated by the null terminator character '\0' (ASCII 0x0). String handling functions like strlen, strcpy, strcmp, etc. use the null terminator to determine where the string data ends. Without it, string handling functions can read past the intended memory, leading to undefined behavior.

Similarly, in gdb, when printing a string or examining a memory address as a string (using x/s <addr>), both the printf and examine commands also rely on the null terminator to determine where a string ends. However, sometimes programs store strings without a null terminator, and their functions use a length parameter instead to indicate the length of a string.
